title: The tannaim
hook: the sages of the Mishnah, from Hillel's time to Rabbi Judah the Prince

segments.voice: Yesterday, why it was written down, and your line: write it before it's lost. Did you ask someone older for one thing only they remember? Today, the people whose words were saved. Day one thousand sixty-five.

Open the Mishnah almost anywhere and you'll hear a room full of people. Rabbi Meir says this. Rabbi Judah says that. Rabbi Shimon disagrees. And the sages say something else. The house of Shammai, the house of Hillel. Rabban Gamaliel, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Eliezer. The book reads less like a rulebook and more like the minutes of a very long meeting, with everyone's name attached to what they said. These are the teachers of the Mishnah. The Talmud has a single word for each of them, and it's today's word.
screen: `RABBI MEIR SAYS. RABBI JUDAH SAYS.` → `A ROOM FULL OF NAMES.` → `ONE WORD FOR EACH OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Tanna. In the plural, tannaim. It's an Aramaic word, and Jastrow's dictionary of Talmudic Aramaic ties it to repeating, and so to teaching, because this teaching was learned by saying it over and over. The tannaim are the sages of the Mishnah, from the time of Hillel and Shammai down to Rabbi Judah the Prince, who gathered their words. Hillel, patient. Shammai, strict. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who rebuilt after the Temple fell. Rabbi Akiva. And Rabbi Meir, a name the Talmud reads as one who gives light. The Talmud, in tractate Eruvin, says that wasn't even his given name. He was called Meir because he lit up the eyes of the sages in the law. Now something surprising about all those names. The Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, says that a teaching in the Mishnah with no name on it follows Rabbi Meir, and then adds: and all of them follow Rabbi Akiva, his teacher. So even the unsigned lines have a teacher behind them, and a teacher behind him. Here's a second surprise. In the Talmud the same word, tanna, also names a different job: a reciter in the house of study who had memorized great stores of teachings and could repeat them on request. And the Talmud teases them. In tractate Sotah it says, in paraphrase, the tanna recites and doesn't know what he's saying. Repeating the words wasn't the same as understanding them. Which sets up tomorrow. The tannaim gave the teaching its words. Someone still had to explain them.
screen: `TANNA: ONE WHO REPEATS, AND TEACHES.` · `HILLEL TO RABBI JUDAH THE PRINCE.` · `MEIR: HE LIT UP THE SAGES' EYES.` · `UNSIGNED LINES STILL HAVE A TEACHER.` · then, large: `THE TEACHERS OF THE MISHNAH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one tanna's name. Take Rabbi Meir, the one who gave light. Sit, and breathe. On the in-breath, think Rabbi. On the out-breath, Meir. Let the name settle the way a tanna would have settled a teaching, by repeating it until it's yours. Then, for the rest of the bell, think of someone who lit up a subject for you: a teacher, a parent, a coworker who explained the thing nobody else could. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Tanna. A teacher of the Mishnah, one of the sages from Hillel's time to Rabbi Judah the Prince, tied in the dictionary to repeating. Today's word.
Your line: the teachers of the mishnah. Today, when you repeat something you learned from someone, say their name with it. Day one thousand sixty-five.

howItsDone: When Jews study the Mishnah they quote it by its teachers, saying 'Rabbi Meir says' or 'the sages say', and it is a custom to repeat a teaching in the name of the one who said it.

fork.setup: you're a student in an ancient house of study. you can recite a whole tractate word for word, but you can't explain a line of it. what would the Talmud call you?
options: a tanna who doesn't know what he's saying.
fork.reveal: the Talmud in Sotah teases it: the tanna recites and doesn't know what he says. memory alone wasn't understanding.

original.note: Aramaic: a teacher of the Mishnah; plural tannaim, תַּנָּאִים.

trapdoor: what you thought: tannaim is just a fancy word for old rabbis.
what it means: the teachers of the Mishnah, from Hillel's time to Rabbi Judah the Prince, whose names fill its pages.
what a scholar hears: an Aramaic word for repeating that names both the sages and the academy reciters, and Sanhedrin 86a's chain: an unsigned mishnah is Rabbi Meir, and all follow Rabbi Akiva.

sources.ref: Marcus Jastrow, A Dictionary of the Targumim, the Talmud Babli and Yerushalmi, and the Midrashic Literature (1903), s.v. tana, tanna

notes: Tanna: the link to 'repeat, teach' is attributed to Jastrow's dictionary (cited). Please confirm the entry supports it.

Eruvin 13b paraphrased: Rabbi Meir's name was not Meir (the Talmud says it was Nehorai); he was called Meir because he enlightened the eyes of the sages in halakhah. 'Whose name means one who gives light' is the Talmud's own reading. Please confirm.
Sanhedrin 86a paraphrased (Rabbi Yochanan's statement): an unattributed mishnah is Rabbi Meir, and all follow Rabbi Akiva. Please confirm.
Sotah 22a paraphrased: the tanna recites and does not know what he says. The teaching that 'tanna' also names the academy reciter is stated; please confirm.
One-word sketches (Hillel patient, Shammai strict, Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuilt after the Temple fell) summarize earlier days; please confirm they are fair.
Range 'from the time of Hillel and Shammai down to Rabbi Judah the Prince' follows the outline; no dates given.
Editor: removed the superlative 'the standard dictionary' (now names Jastrow, the cited source); Meir's meaning now attributed to the Talmud's reading.
